implementation_notes: Channels are a Go primitive and the language's headline feature. The runtime implements one as an hchan holding a circular buffer (dataqsiz, sendx, recvx), a closed flag, and two wait queues of parked goroutines, guarded by a mutex. The key semantics from the memory model: a send is synchronised before the matching receive completes, so the channel carries a happens-before edge and no lock is needed on the payload. The buffer capacity is the design decision: make(chan T) is a rendezvous (a pure synchronisation point), make(chan T, n) bounds the sender at n. select waits on several channel operations at once, picking a random ready case (so it does not starve) and locking the channels in address order (so two selects cannot deadlock), with a nil channel blocking forever - which is the idiom for disabling a case in a loop. Directional types (chan<- T, <-chan T) make the multiplicity contract a compile-time check.
idiom_name: make(chan T[, n]) with send/receive, close, select; directional channel types enforce multiplicity
pitfalls: Never closing: every consumer's range-loop blocks forever after the producer exits - the classic goroutine leak.
Send on a closed channel panics; close a closed channel panics; close a nil channel panics. With multiple senders, a coordinator must close after a WaitGroup.
A nil channel blocks forever on send and receive - the idiom for disabling a select case, and an unreviewed footgun elsewhere.

Blocking on an unbuffered channel with no counterpart parks the goroutine (and, if every goroutine is parked, the runtime reports 'all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!'; a partial deadlock just hangs).
select picks a RANDOM ready case, so a loop with a fast-ready case can spin - select is for multiplexing rare events and timeouts, not a hot polling loop.

A channel operation is a mutex lock plus a queue push plus a possible wakeup: routing shared-state reads through channels makes them a slower mutex. Use a channel to transfer ownership, a mutex for shared state.
